patches.old: This is the **Dickens-Flynn model** logic: when environments are more uniform, genetic differences explain more of the remaining variance.
patches.new: This pattern is the **Scarr-Rowe effect**, named for the investigators who first reported and replicated it and brought back to prominence by Turkheimer and colleagues in 2003: when environments are more uniform, genetic differences explain more of the remaining variance, so heritability rises with socioeconomic status. (The separate **Dickens-Flynn model** addresses a different puzzle — how heritability can be high while environmental effects such as the Flynn effect are also large — by proposing that small genetic advantages get multiplied through the environments people select and evoke.)

sources.title: Turkheimer, Haley, Waldron, D'Onofrio and Gottesman, Psychological Science 2003 — socioeconomic status modifies heritability of IQ in young children
Nisbett and colleagues, on the Scarr-Rowe interaction between measured socioeconomic status and the heritability of cognitive ability

visual.title: The curve, the theories and the statistic
visual.alt: A normal IQ distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, marked at 70, 85, 100, 115 and 130 with the clinical cut-offs two deviations out; four cards summarising Spearman, Cattell, Gardner and Sternberg; and a two-column list separating what heritability is — a share of variance in one population in one environment — from what it is not, including any claim about an individual or about a gap between groups.
visual.caption: Heritability describes variance inside one population in one environment. The fact that the number itself drops under deprivation is the clearest sign it is not a fixed property of the trait.
